issues: Subhavastu River (蘇婆薩堵河) → the Life writes 蘇婆薩堵, i.e. Suvāstu (as DM itself has in 03.01); Śubhavastu is the Xiyu ji's 蘇婆伐窣堵
en_revised: Traveling north from the city, he climbed over mountains and crossed rivers for more than six hundred li, entering the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國), which lies along the Suvāstu River (蘇婆薩堵河).

issues: Mount Hila (醯羅山; Hidda) → the gloss 'Hidda' is not in the Chinese and misleads (Hidda is 醯羅城 near Nagarahāra); 醯羅山 is the Swat hill
en_revised: Traveling more than four hundred li south of the city, one reaches Mount Hila (醯羅山), which is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life, having heard half a stanza, abandoned his body to repay the kindness of a yakṣa.

issues: The King of Uḍḍiyāna (烏地王) → 烏地王 is Udita (烏地多), the North Indian king escorting him on the return from Prayāga, not the king of Uḍḍiyāna (Beal: Udhita-raja); the passage is the return journey, setting out from Jālandhara; they returned following the Master → they came back in the Master's company (依法師而還)
en_revised: King Udita (烏地王) sent men to escort him, and after traveling westward for more than twenty days, they reached the country of Siṃhapura (僧訶補羅國). At that time, there were more than a hundred monks, all of whom were northerners, who were carrying scriptures, statues, and other items, and they came back in the Master's company.

issues: Rājapura (曷邏闍補羅國) → the Life writes 遏邏闍補羅國 (the Xiyu ji 曷邏闍補羅)
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Rājapura (遏邏闍補羅國).

issues: Paramārthasaptati (勝義諦論) → Paramārthasatya-śāstra (as DM in 04.01.02); country of Tsekia (礫迦國) → same country as the Ṭakka (礫迦國) of the first sentence (the Life writes 礫 for 磔 throughout)
en_revised: From here, he traveled southeast, descending the mountains and crossing waters for over seven hundred *li*, until he reached the country of Ṭakka (礫迦國). From Lampaka (藍波) to this land, because the people lived in frontier and desolate regions, their customs, clothing, and language differed slightly from those of India, and they possessed a vulgar and uncouth air. After departing the country of Rājapura (曷邏闍補羅國), he traveled for three days, crossed the Candrabhāgā River (栴達羅婆伽河), and arrived at the city of Jayapura (闍耶補羅城), where he stayed at a heretical monastery. The monastery was located outside the west gate of the city; at this time, his companions numbered over twenty people. The following day, he advanced to the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城). Within the city was a monastery with over one hundred monks, where in the past the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu had composed the *Paramārthasatya-śāstra* (勝義諦論). Beside it was a *stūpa* two hundred feet high, which was a place where the four past Buddhas had preached the Dharma, and traces of their walking meditation could still be seen. Departing from here, he left the city of Narasiṃha (那羅僧訶城) and traveled east into a great Palāśa forest, where he encountered a band of over fifty robbers. The robbers plundered all the clothing and goods belonging to the Master and his companions, and then brandished their knives to drive them toward a dry pond south of the road, intending to slaughter them all. The pond was overgrown with brambles and creepers; the novice monk accompanying the Master peered through the thorny thicket and saw a water hole on the southern bank of the pond large enough for a person to pass through. He privately informed the Master, and they escaped through it together. They ran hurriedly to the southeast for about two or three li and met a Brahmin (婆羅門) tilling the land. They informed him that they had been robbed; upon hearing this, he was shocked and immediately unyoked his oxen to give to the Master. He then blew a conch and beat a drum toward the village to summon help, gathering over eighty men who each took up weapons and rushed to the site of the robbers. When the robbers saw the crowd, they fled and scattered into the forest. The Master then went to the pond to untie the bonds of his companions, and having received clothes from the villagers to distribute among them, they went together to the village to stay the night. The others wept in sorrow, but the Master alone smiled, free from worry or grief. His companions asked him, "Our clothing and provisions for the journey have been completely plundered by the robbers; only our lives remain, and we have barely survived. We are exhausted and in dire straits, and the situation could not be worse. When we think back on what happened in the forest, we cannot help but feel sad. Why is it that you, Master, do not share in this worry, but instead smile with joy?" He replied, "The value of existence lies solely in life. Since life remains, what else is there to worry about? Therefore, a popular book in my homeland says: 'The greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life.' As long as life exists, the greatest treasure is not lost. Why should one worry or grieve over mere trifles like clothing and provisions?" Because of this, his companions were moved to realization. Such was the clarity of his mind, which remained unclouded even when stirred. The next day, they arrived at the eastern border of the country of Ṭakka (礫迦國) and reached a large city. To the west of the city and north of the road was a large mango grove, in which lived a Brahman seven hundred years of age. Yet when one looked at him, he appeared to be only about thirty, with a stalwart physique and a profound, discerning mind; he was well-versed in the *Madhyamaka* (中論) and *Śata* (百論) treatises and proficient in the *Vedas* and other such books. He had two attendants, each over one hundred years old. The Master met with him, and they received one another with great joy. Having also learned that the Master had been robbed, the Brahman immediately dispatched an attendant to order the Buddhist laypeople in the city to prepare food for him. The city had several thousand households, but those who believed in the Buddha were few, while those who followed non-Buddhist paths were very numerous. When the Master had been in Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅), his reputation had already spread far and wide and was known to all countries. The messenger went throughout the city and announced: "A monk from the land of China has arrived; he was robbed by bandits nearby and all his clothes are gone; it is time for you all to know this." Moved by the power of his merit, the heretical parties reformed their hearts. More than three hundred prominent people, upon hearing the news, each brought a piece of patterned cotton cloth along with food and drink, arriving respectfully to pile them before him, bowing and kneeling to inquire after his well-being. The Master offered blessings for them and explained the retribution of cause and effect, causing all those people to generate the intention for the path, abandon the false, and return to the true; they returned home laughing, talking, and dancing with joy. The elderly teacher sighed at this, saying it was something that had never happened before. The Master then distributed the cotton cloth among the others, and each person received enough for several suits of clothing; as there was still a surplus, fifty pieces of cloth were offered to the elderly teacher. He remained there for one month to study the *Śata-śāstra* (經百論) and the *Śata-śāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論). This person was a disciple of Nāgārjuna (龍猛) and had received the teachings directly from his master; his explanations were exceptionally clear and pure.

issues: Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達羅國) → the Life writes 闍爛達那國
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達那國). Upon entering the country, he went to the Nāgaradhana Monastery (那伽羅馱那寺), where there was a virtuous monk named Candravarman, who was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. He therefore stayed there for four months to study the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-vibhāṣā* (眾事分毘婆沙).

issues: such as Śāriputra and others → the Chinese names Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana (舍利子、沒特伽羅子等塔皆現在); DM drops Maudgalyāyana from the list
en_revised: From here, traveling east for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Mathurā (秣菟羅國). The stupas containing the remains of the holy disciples of the Śākya Tathāgata, such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), are all still present. These include the stupas of Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra (呾麗衍尼弗呾羅), Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula, and Mañjuśrī. On the annual days of merit-making, the monastic community gathers at these various stupas to perform offerings according to their respective traditions. Those who study the Abhidharma make offerings to Śāriputra; those who practice meditation make offerings to Maudgalyāyana; those who recite and uphold the sutras make offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (滿慈子); those who study the Vinaya make offerings to Upāli; the bhikṣuṇīs make offerings to Ānanda; those who have not yet received the full ordination make offerings to Rāhula; and those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various bodhisattvas.

issues: Śrughna (窣祿勤那國) → the Life writes 祿勒那國; traveling east → 東行 as in the Life (the Xiyu ji has 東北行); traveling east from the river → 又河東行: the river is the Yamunā (Xiyu ji 閻牟那河東行)
en_revised: Traveling east for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Śrughna (祿勒那國). It borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east, rests against great mountains to the north, and the Yamunā River flows through the middle of its territory. Traveling east from the river [Yamunā] for over eight hundred li, one reaches the source of the Gaṅgā, which is three or four li wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, it is over ten li wide. Its water tastes sweet and delicious, and fine sand flows with the current. Local records call it the "Water of Merit." They say that if one bathes in it, one’s sins and transgressions are eradicated; if one sips its waves or rinses one’s mouth with its flow, then calamities and disasters are extinguished; and those who drown and die in it are immediately reborn in heaven to enjoy blessings. Foolish men and women constantly gather on the riverbank, but these are all heterodox, erroneous claims without any reality. Later, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) demonstrated the correct principles, and only then did these practices cease. The country has a great virtuous master named Jayagupta (闍耶毱多), who is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. The Dharma Master stayed for one winter and half of spring to listen to the *Vibhāṣā* of the Sautrāntika school until it was completed.

issues: requested the heavenly host to use their supernatural power → 請天軍以神力: 天軍 is the arhat Devasena (提婆犀那) just named, who takes Guṇaprabha up (Beal: Devasena); Abhidharmakośa-bhīṣma-śāstra (俱舍雹論) → 'hailstorm on the Kośa', Kośakarakā-śāstra (Beal: Kosha-karika); he proceeded to follow its practices → 遂依行焉: and it was named accordingly (Beal: accordingly it was so done)
en_revised: Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國). Its king is of the Śūdra caste. There are more than ten monasteries and over eight hundred monks, all of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna. Four or five li to the south of the great city, there is a small monastery with more than fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (瞿拏鉢剌婆) composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling more than one hundred works. The master of treatises was a native of the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國); he originally studied the Mahāyāna but later turned to study the Hīnayāna. At that time, the arhat Devasena (提婆犀那) traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya (慈氏) to resolve various doubts and hesitations, so he requested Devasena (天軍) to use his supernatural power to take him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya, he bowed but did not prostrate, saying, "I am a monk who has received the full precepts, while Maitreya dwells in the heavens like a worldly being; it is not appropriate for me to pay homage." He went back and forth three times in this manner, and each time he failed to offer prostrations. Because he was arrogant and self-important, his doubts remained unresolved. Three or four li to the south of Guṇaprabha’s monastery, there is another monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna. This is the place where the master of treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) ended his life. The master of treatises was originally a native of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國); he was widely learned and possessed great talent, and he was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā* of the Sarvāstivāda school. At that time, the bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親), also possessing profound wisdom and extensive learning, had previously composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), which refuted the tenets held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā*. Its principles were profound and its language elegant; there was no student in the Western Regions who did not praise and admire it, and even the ghosts and spirits all studied and practiced it. Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) read it and was filled with indignation. For another twelve years, he pondered deeply and composed the *Kośakarakā-śāstra* (俱舍雹論, 'Hailstorm on the Kośa') in twenty-five thousand verses and eight hundred thousand words. Once finished, he wished to meet with Vasubandhu (世親) to determine who was right and who was wrong, but he died before he could do so. Later, when Vasubandhu saw his treatise, he sighed at his understanding and insight, saying that his power of thought was not inferior to the masters of the *Vibhāṣā*. "However," he added, "it is very much in accordance with my own tenets; it should be named the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論)," and this was done accordingly. After Saṃghabhadra died, a stūpa was erected in the Āmra forest (菴沒羅林) in his honor, which can still be seen today. Beside the forest is another stūpa, which is the place where the remains of the Śāstra Master Vimalamitra (毘末羅蜜多羅) were deposited. The Śāstra Master was a native of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國); he had entered the monastic order in the Sarvāstivāda school and traveled throughout the five Indias, exhausting his studies of the Tripiṭaka. As he was about to return to his home country, he passed by the stūpa of Saṃghabhadra and, grieving that the latter’s writings had not yet been widely propagated before he suddenly passed away, he vowed to compose further treatises to refute the Mahāyāna doctrines, extinguish the name of Vasubandhu, and ensure that the Master’s tenets would be transmitted for ages to come. Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and blood flowed over his entire body. Realizing that this suffering was caused by his evil views, he wrote a confession, urged his companions not to slander the Mahāyāna, and expired as he finished speaking. At the place where he died, the earth sank into a pit. In that country, there was a man of great virtue named Mitrasena, ninety years of age, who was a disciple of the Śāstra Master Guṇaprabha (德光) and was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. The Master then spent half a spring and one summer studying the *Tattvasandeśa-śāstra* (怛埵三弟鑠論) and the *Anujñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (隨發智論) of the Sarvāstivāda school, among other works.

issues: Ahicchattra (堊醯掣呾羅國) → the Life writes 醯掣怛羅國 (without 堊)
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Ahicchattra (醯掣怛羅國).

issues: two hundred li → 二百餘里, more than two hundred li; bearing 東行 east (the Xiyu ji has 東南行)
en_revised: Traveling east again for more than two hundred li, he reached the country of Kapitha (劫比他國).

issues: At the top stands a vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → 上起精舍: on top a vihāra has been built; the Sanskrit gloss is not in the Chinese; they appear to be seventy-odd feet high → 見高七十餘尺: they now stand over seventy feet high; 面東西下 'facing east, descending' kept (the phrase is odd; the Xiyu ji has 東面下); the Life places the monastery 城東二十餘里, east of the city (Beal: east; the CBETA Xiyu ji text in places.tsv has 城西)
en_revised: More than twenty *li* to the east of the city is a great monastery (saṃghārāma). Within the courtyard are the Three Precious Stairs (Devāvatāra), arranged from north to south and facing east, descending. This is the place where the Buddha, having finished preaching the Dharma for Lady Māyā in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, descended to the Jambudvīpa continent. The middle [stair] is of gold, the left is of crystal, and the right is of white silver. When the Tathāgata arose from the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharma-sabhā), he led the host of deities and stepped down the middle stairs. The Great Brahmā King, holding a white whisk, trod upon the silver stairs and took his place on the right; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, holding a precious canopy, stepped upon the crystal stairs and took his place on the left. At that time, hundreds of thousands of deities and great bodhisattvas accompanied him as he descended. Until a few hundred years ago, the original stairs still existed, but now they have all sunk and disappeared. Later kings, out of longing and reverence, piled up bricks and stones to imitate their form, decorating them with various jewels, and they now stand over seventy feet high. On top a vihāra (精舍) has been built, in which there is a stone Buddha image, with images of Śakra and Brahmā on the left and right, all modeled after the original arrangement, so as to manifest as if they were truly present. Beside it is a stone pillar seven *zhang* high, erected by King Aśoka (Aśoka-rāja). Nearby is a stone foundation, over fifty paces long and seven feet high; this is the place where the Buddha formerly walked in meditation (caṅkramaṇa).

issues: lured him and killed him → the victim of Śaśāṅka is the elder brother Rājyavardhana (共立其弟 follows); the Life's 喜增在位仁慈 literally names Harṣa (Beal likewise), whereas the Xiyu ji has 王增 here; DM's wording makes Harṣa the murdered king
en_revised: From here, traveling northwest for two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國). The country is four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and five to six li in width. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles. The king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (曷利沙伐彈那). His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (波羅羯邏伐彈那), and his late elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (遏羅闍伐彈那). Harṣavardhana is benevolent in his reign, and the people of the country praise him. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) of the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國) in East India, fearing his intelligence and strategy and regarding him as a threat to his borders, lured his elder brother and killed him. The high minister Bhaṇi (婆尼) and the other officials, grieving that the common people were without a master, together installed his younger brother, Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多), to inherit the ancestral temple. The king possessed a heroic and outstanding bearing, his strategic plans were grand and far-reaching, his virtue moved heaven and earth, and his righteousness affected gods and men; thus he was able to avenge his brother and bring all of India under his control. Wherever his majesty reached or his civilizing influence touched, all people submitted to his virtue. Once the world was settled and the common people were at peace, he put away his weapons and ceased hostilities to cultivate meritorious deeds. He decreed that no life be taken within his borders and ordered all his subjects to abstain from eating meat. Wherever there were sacred sites, he built saṃghārāmas, and every year for twenty-one days he provided offerings to the entire community of monks. Every five years he held a great Mokṣa-mahāpariṣad (無遮大會), where he distributed all the accumulated wealth of his treasury as alms; examining his conduct, he is of the same class as Sudāna (須達拏). To the northwest of the city there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, and six or seven li to the southeast, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high; both were built by King Aśoka, and both are places where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma. The Dharma Master entered this country and arrived at the Bhadra-vihāra (跋達邏毘訶羅寺), where he stayed for three months; under the guidance of the Tripiṭaka master Vīryasena (毘離耶犀那), he finished reading the *Buddhadūta-vibhāṣā* (佛使毘婆沙) and the *Sūryavarman-vibhāṣā* (日胄毘婆沙).

issues: worshipping the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) and the images at Gṛdhrakūṭa → 禮菩提樹像耆闍崛山: the image at the Bodhi tree and Gṛdhrakūṭa; we wish to accept your repentance → 願受懺悔: we pray you to accept our repentance
en_revised: After paying homage to the sacred sites in the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國), the Master sailed eastward down the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) in a boat with over eighty people, intending to go to the country of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國). After traveling about one hundred li, both banks of the river were found to be covered in a forest of aśoka trees, which were exceptionally deep and lush. From within the forest on both banks, more than ten pirate boats suddenly emerged, rowing against the current. There was great alarm on the boat, and several people threw themselves into the river. The pirates then forced the boat to the bank and ordered everyone to remove their clothes so they could search for treasures.  These pirates were long-time worshippers of the goddess Durgā (突伽天神), and every autumn they would seek a person of handsome appearance to kill, using his flesh and blood as a sacrifice to pray for good fortune. Seeing that the Master’s appearance was grand and his physique was suitable, they looked at each other with joy and said, "The time for our sacrifice is almost over and we have not been able to find anyone; now this śramaṇa has a refined and beautiful appearance, would it not be auspicious to kill him for the sacrifice!"  The Master replied, "If my humble body, Zang, can serve as a sacrifice, I truly would not begrudge it. However, I have come from afar with the intention of worshipping the image at the Bodhi tree (菩提樹像) and Gṛdhrakūṭa (耆闍崛山), as well as seeking instruction in the scriptures and the Dharma. If you donors kill me before this wish is fulfilled, I fear it will not bring you good fortune." All the people on the boat joined in the plea, and some even wished to offer their own bodies in his stead, but the pirates would not allow it. Thereupon, the bandit chief sent men to fetch water, cleared a space in a flower grove to set up an altar, and mixed mud to plaster and sweep it. He ordered two men to draw their swords and drag the Master onto the altar, intending to strike him immediately. The Master’s countenance showed no fear, which astonished all the bandits. Realizing that he could not escape, he said to the bandits, "I pray you grant me a short time; do not press or harass me, so that I may calmly and joyfully meet my end." The Master then concentrated his mind on the Tuṣita Palace (覩史多宮) and meditated on Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), vowing to be reborn there to pay reverent homage and make offerings, to receive the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽師地論), to hear the wonderful Dharma, and to achieve supernatural wisdom; thereafter, he would return to be reborn in this world to transform these men, leading them to practice superior deeds, abandon all evil karma, and widely proclaim all Dharmas for the benefit and peace of all beings. He then bowed to the Buddhas of the ten directions, sat in correct mindfulness, and focused his heart on Maitreya, without any other distractions. In his contemplation, it was as if he had ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山) and passed through the first, second, and third heavens, seeing Maitreya Bodhisattva at the Wonderful Precious Terrace in the Tuṣita Palace, surrounded by a multitude of heavenly beings. At this time, his body and mind were joyful; he did not even know he was on the altar, nor did he remember there were bandits. His companions began to wail aloud. In an instant, a black wind rose from all sides, snapping trees and sending sand flying; the river surged with waves, and the boats were overturned. The bandits were greatly terrified and asked his companions, "Where does this śramaṇa come from? What is his name?" They replied, "This is the one who has come from the country of China (支那國) to seek the Dharma. If you gentlemen kill him, you will incur immeasurable sin." "Observe the state of the wind and waves; the heavenly deities are already enraged, so you should quickly repent." The bandits were afraid and, leading one another, offered repentance and apologies, bowing their heads in refuge. At that time, he was still unaware of what had happened; the bandits touched him with their hands, and only then did he open his eyes and say to the bandits, "Has the time come?" The bandits replied, "We dare not harm the Master; we pray you to accept our repentance." The Dharma Master accepted their salutations and apologies, and for them he explained the unwholesome deeds of killing, stealing, and heterodox sacrifices, and the suffering of the uninterrupted hells that they would endure in the future. "Why, for the sake of a body as brief as a flash of lightning or morning dew, do you plant the seeds for an *asaṃkhyeya* (immeasurable) duration of suffering?" The bandits knocked their heads to the ground and thanked him, saying, "We were deluded by false thoughts, doing what should not be done and engaging in matters that should not be engaged in. If we had not encountered the Master, whose merit and virtue moved the dark spirits, how could we have heard such instruction? We request that from this day forward we shall cease these deeds; we pray that the Master will bear witness." Thereupon, they exhorted one another, gathered all their plundered goods and threw them into the river, returned all the clothing and property they had seized to their original owners, and together received the five precepts. The wind and waves then returned to calm. The crowd of bandits was joyful, and they bowed their heads to take their leave. His companions’ respect and admiration for him became even more extraordinary than before. Those who heard of this, both far and near, were all filled with wonder and astonishment. If his earnestness in seeking the Dharma had not been so profound, how could this have been brought about? From here, he traveled eastward for more than three hundred *li*, crossed the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, and arrived north at the country of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國).

issues: to defeat the heretics of the Lesser Vehicle → 挫小乘外道: to defeat the Hīnayānists and the heretics (Xiyu ji 挫小乘，伏外道)
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred li, crossing to the south of the Gaṅgā River and the north of the Yamunā River, one reaches the country of Prayāga (鉢羅耶伽國). To the southwest of the city, in a grove of campaka flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Buddha formerly subdued the heretics. Beside it is a saṃghārāma, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva composed the *Śataśāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論) to defeat the followers of the Lesser Vehicle and the heretics. To the east of the great city, at the confluence of the two rivers, there is a level ground to the west, fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; the land is flat and even. Since ancient times, kings and noble families who were benevolent and charitable have all come here, and for this reason, the place is called the Great Alms Ground. The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) also follows this tradition, accumulating wealth for five years and distributing it in seventy-five days; from the Triple Gem above down to the solitary and the poor, there is no one to whom he does not give.

issues: Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā (顯揚論) → 顯揚論 is the Xianyang shengjiao lun, *Prakaraṇāryavācā (as DM in 05.02)
en_revised: From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one frequently encounters fierce beasts and wild elephants. After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國). There are more than ten monasteries and over three hundred monks. Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) over sixty feet high, containing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王). Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven spending the summer retreat preaching the Dharma to his mother, the king, longing for him, requested Maudgalyāyana to take a skillful craftsman up to heaven to observe the Buddha’s venerable countenance and demeanor. Upon returning, he carved a likeness of the true form out of red sandalwood, and when the World-Honored One descended, the statue went to welcome the Buddha; this is that very image.  To the south of the city is an old residence, which is the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (瞿史羅長者). Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery, which is the elder’s garden. Within it is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). To the southeast is a multi-storied pavilion, which is the place where Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論). Further to the east, in an mango grove, are the old foundations of the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (無著菩薩) composed the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚論).

issues: Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā (顯揚論) → 顯揚論 is the Xianyang shengjiao lun, *Prakaraṇāryavācā (as DM in 05.02)
en_revised: To the south of the city is an old residence, which is the former home of the Elder Ghoṣila (瞿史羅). Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery (saṃghārāma), which is the garden of the Elder. Within it is a stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). To the southeast is a multi-storied pavilion, which is the place where Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論). Further to the east, in an Āmra grove (菴沒羅林), is an old foundation, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (無著) composed the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚論).

issues: Eight hundred paces → 八百餘步, more than eight hundred paces (DM's 06.01 has it right)
en_revised: Five or six li to the south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). Formerly it was a monastery, but now it has fallen into ruin. To the left and right of the east gate, stone pillars were erected, each over seventy feet high, which were established by King Aśoka (無憂王). All the buildings have been destroyed, with only one brick chamber remaining, in which there is a golden image. In the past, when the Buddha ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit (勝軍王) felt a longing for him; hearing that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image, he had this one made. Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetic killed a woman to slander the Buddha. Over one hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多) attempted to harm the Buddha with poison and fell into hell in his physical body. To the south of that is another large pit, the place where the bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) slandered the Buddha and fell into hell in his physical body. More than eight hundred paces to the south of this pit is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) slandered the Buddha and fell into hell in her physical body. Looking into these three pits, one cannot see the bottom. Seventy-odd paces to the east of the monastery is a large and tall mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍). Inside is a Buddha image seated facing east, the place where the Tathāgata formerly engaged in debate with non-Buddhists. Next to the east is a deva temple, equal in size to the mūla-gandha-kuṭī; as the sunlight shifts, the shadow of the deva temple never reaches the mūla-gandha-kuṭī, while the shadow of the mūla-gandha-kuṭī always covers the deva temple. Three or four li further to the east is a stūpa, the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) engaged in debate with non-Buddhists.

issues: traveling over one hundred li to the Ganges, he arrived at Śvetapura → 去殑伽河百餘里 is ambiguous: 'going 100+ li toward/along the Ganges' (DM; Beal: following the Ganges for 100 li) or 'at 100+ li from the Ganges'; DM's reading kept; the Life writes 吠多補羅 (no 濕)
en_revised: From the southern border of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐), traveling over one hundred li to the Ganges (殑伽河) River, he arrived at the city of Śvetapura (吠多補羅城), where he obtained the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra* (菩薩藏經).
